summary:
The Astronaut Health Monitoring System is an educational prototype that shows how an astronaut’s health could be monitored on long space missions. It is a local web dashboard built by Team Bricks (Muhammad Zohaib, Abdullah Saeed, Obaidullah Shahid and Syed Muhammad Hassan Raza).

It combines five modules:

Mission Control HUD: replayed wearable telemetry (heart rate, HRV, respiration, skin conductance, skin temperature) scored by machine-learning models for stress and anomalies, with scenarios such as spacewalk, cognitive crisis and hypoxia.
Camera pulse demo: an experimental pulse estimate from forehead pixels in a webcam feed, processed in the browser.
Gravity and environment simulator: modeled effects of Earth, zero-g, Moon and Mars conditions.
Mars 3D Expedition Center: an illustrative 3D view of the same scenario outputs.
921-analyte explorer: real Inspiration4 blood biomarker trends from NASA OSD-575.

It is built with Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn), a local API server, SQLite, and a browser interface with live charts and 3D graphics. The stress model is gradient boosting (5-fold group cross-validation 0.940) and the anomaly detector is Isolation Forest.

Camera video never leaves the browser, and all data stays local. Every panel is labeled as a demo, and the system is not validated for medical or flight use.
details:
What it does and how it works
The Astronaut Health Monitoring System is a local web dashboard that brings spaceflight health data, simulated telemetry and mission-environment models into one console. It has five modules:

  • Mission Control HUD: replays WESAD-derived telemetry (heart rate, HRV, respiration, skin conductance, skin temperature). It shows a health score, a stress probability and an anomaly score, and lets users inject scenarios such as spacewalk, cognitive crisis and hypoxia.
  • Camera pulse demo: estimates pulse from forehead pixels in the browser camera (rPPG). Video stays in the browser and only RGB averages go to the local server.
  • Gravity and environment simulator: shows modeled changes for Earth, zero-g, Moon and Mars conditions.
  • Mars 3D Expedition Center: a 3D Mars and human-figure view of the same scenario outputs.
  • 921-analyte explorer: charts Inspiration4 biomarker trends from NASA OSD-575, from before launch to return.

Benefits and intended impact
Space health data is usually scattered and hard to read. The console makes it easy to explore and teach, and to show how stress, gravity and radiation could be monitored on long missions. It is an educational and research starting point, not a medical tool.

Tools
Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn, joblib), a local API server, SQLite, a browser dashboard with live charts, webcam access and 3D graphics. Data comes from NASA OSD-575 and WESAD. The models are gradient boosting (5-fold group cross-validation 0.940) and Isolation Forest.

Creativity
It combines real NASA biomarker data, a camera-based pulse estimate that needs no extra hardware, and 3D scenario views in one mission-control interface.

Factors we considered

  • Privacy: camera video is never uploaded, and everything runs on the local machine.
  • Honesty: the camera demo shows HRV and respiration as “not measured” rather than guessing, and every panel is labeled as a demo.
  • Safety: the prototype is not validated for medical or flight use and must not be used to diagnose or make safety decisions.
